groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
Almost everyone has delayed an important task, such as studying for an exam, even when they knew the delay would cause trouble later. This habit is called procrastination. It is often blamed on laziness or poor time management, but many psychologists now believe that the real cause lies elsewhere.

According to this view, procrastination is mainly a way of managing emotions. A difficult task can produce unpleasant feelings, including boredom, anxiety, and doubt about one's own ability. Turning to something more enjoyable, like watching videos, brings immediate relief. The human mind also tends to value rewards that come now more than rewards that come later, so the comfort of the present moment easily outweighs a distant deadline. The relief is temporary, however, and the unfinished work usually returns with added stress and guilt.

Understanding this cycle suggests practical remedies. Dividing a large project into small steps makes the first step less frightening, and removing distractions, for example by switching off a phone, reduces temptation. Surprisingly, being kind to oneself also seems to help. In one study, students who forgave themselves for delaying their preparation for an exam procrastinated less before the next one. Harsh self-criticism, by contrast, tends to increase the negative feelings that led to the delay in the first place.

groups.title: Read an Academic Passage
groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
In regions with distinct seasons, a tree adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark every year. Rapid growth in spring produces pale wood, while slower growth late in the summer leaves a thin, dark band. Together, the two form one annual ring, so counting the rings of a trunk reveals the tree's age. The rings record far more than age, however.

Because trees grow more in favorable years, a wide ring generally indicates plentiful rain and a narrow one drought or cold. Trees throughout a region therefore share a similar sequence of wide and narrow rings. By matching the pattern in a living tree with the overlapping pattern in older wood, such as beams from historic buildings, researchers can extend the record back thousands of years. This technique has allowed archaeologists to date ancient wooden structures to the very year their timber was cut, and it has given climate scientists a year-by-year account of past droughts.

The method is not without shortcomings. Many tropical trees, which grow throughout the year, form no clear annual rings. Moreover, a narrow ring is ambiguous: it may reflect a dry year, but an insect attack or the shade of a taller neighbor can stunt growth as well. For this reason, scientists avoid drawing conclusions from a single tree and compare samples from many trees instead.

questions.explanation: The professor explains echolocation: calls, echoes and what the bat learns from them.
questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?

listening.script: OK, let's start with a puzzle. How does an animal catch a tiny flying insect in complete darkness? Bats do it hundreds of times a night. And no, it's not because they have amazing eyes. By the way, bats aren't blind. That's a myth. But in the dark, they rely on something else, called echolocation. Here's how it works. As a bat flies, it sends out very short, very high calls. Most of them are too high for human ears, so to us the night seems quiet. When a call hits an object, say, a moth, an echo bounces back. The bat's brain measures how long that echo took to return. A quick echo means the moth is close. A slower one means it's farther away. And the bat doesn't call at a steady rate. When it's just searching, it might call ten or twenty times a second. But as it closes in on an insect, the calls come faster and faster, up to two hundred a second. Scientists actually call this the feeding buzz. So the bat gets more and more detail exactly when it needs it. Now, the insects aren't helpless. Some moths have ears that can pick up bat calls, and when they hear one, they dive toward the ground. So next time, we'll look at this contest between the hunter and the hunted.

answers: The object is nearby.

options: Why some countries produce more than others
How doctors organize their working day
Why imports are cheaper than local products
Why trading makes countries better off
answers: Why trading makes countries better off
questions.explanation: The talk opens with 'Why do countries trade at all?' and answers it with comparative advantage.
questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the talk?

listening.script: Let's begin with a simple question. Why do countries trade at all? Why doesn't each country just make everything it needs? Well, part of the answer is obvious. Bananas grow easily in Ecuador. They don't grow easily in Norway. So Norway buys bananas, and it sells things like fish and oil. But here's the less obvious part. Trade can help both sides even when one country is better at making everything. This idea goes back to David Ricardo, an English economist writing in the early eighteen hundreds. Economists call it comparative advantage. Let me give you an everyday example. Imagine a doctor who also happens to type faster than her assistant. Should she do her own typing? No. Every hour she spends typing is an hour she isn't seeing patients, and that's where she's most valuable. So she hires the assistant, and they're both better off. Countries work the same way. A country gains by concentrating on what it does best, compared with its other options, and trading for the rest. Now, I'm not saying trade is painless. When cheaper imports arrive, some local factories close, and those workers pay a real price. But for the economy as a whole, most economists agree that specializing and trading leaves countries richer than doing everything alone.

options: To illustrate the benefit of focusing on one's best work
To show that assistants are usually the faster typists
To explain how medical services are traded between countries
To argue that doctors should learn to type faster
answers: To illustrate the benefit of focusing on one's best work
questions.explanation: The doctor types faster but is 'most valuable' seeing patients; 'Countries work the same way.'
questions.prompt: Why does the professor talk about a doctor and her assistant?

listening.script: Think about the last time you heard about a job opening, or an apartment, or even a good film. Who told you? Your best friend? Possibly. But there's a fair chance it was someone you barely know. Back in nineteen seventy-three, the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a wonderfully paradoxical title, The Strength of Weak Ties. By strong ties, he meant close friends and family. Weak ties are acquaintances: an old classmate, a neighbor you nod to. Granovetter had asked people near Boston how they'd found their jobs. And of those who'd heard through a personal contact, most said it was someone they saw only occasionally or rarely. Not a close friend. Why would that be? Well, your close friends know one another. They read the same things and hear the same news, so what they tell you is, more often than not, something you already know. An acquaintance, on the other hand, moves in different circles. She's a bridge to information that would never reach you otherwise. Now, I'm not suggesting close friends don't matter. They're the ones who'll help you move house or sit with you when things go wrong. Weak ties won't do that. But when it comes to fresh information, it's the people at the edge of your social world who tend to deliver.

stages.title: Writing · Academic Discussion

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on business management. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Nakamura
professor.post: This week we are examining how the workplace has changed. In recent years, millions of office employees have started working from home, and many companies have found that the work still gets done. Some firms have since told their staff that they never need to return to the office, while others have called everyone back. I would like to hear your view. Should companies allow employees to work from home permanently? Why or why not?

students.name: Yuki
students.post: I think companies should allow it. My mother used to spend almost three hours a day traveling to and from her office. Now she works from home, and she uses that time to exercise and to have dinner with us. She says she is less tired and gets more done, so both she and her employer benefit.

students.name: Mateus
students.post: I disagree. When everyone works at home all the time, new employees have nobody to learn from. In my first part-time job, I learned the most by watching experienced coworkers and asking quick questions at the next desk. That kind of learning does not happen in a video meeting.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

In my view, companies should let employees work from home permanently if they wish, but they should not close their offices completely. I agree with Yuki that avoiding a long commute gives people more time and energy. However, Mateus makes a fair point about new staff, who need contact with experienced colleagues. I would add an idea that neither of them mentioned: permanent remote work allows a company to hire talented people who live far from its office, including parents of young children and people with disabilities who find daily travel difficult. This makes the workforce more diverse and gives the company a wider choice of candidates. To deal with the problem Mateus describes, firms could bring teams together for a few days each month for training and planning. In this way, employees keep their freedom, and the company keeps its team spirit.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: The last meal I cooked was a simple fried rice, which I made on Sunday evening for my two roommates. We had some rice left from the day before, so I added eggs, carrots, green onions, and a little soy sauce. It took only about fifteen minutes. I chose it because it is cheap and fast, and because I did not want to waste the leftover rice. My roommates said it was delicious, although I think they were just being polite, since I put in too much salt. Anyway, we ate together at the kitchen table and talked for an hour, which was the best part.

listening.script: Thank you for taking part today. Let's start with something simple. Think about the last meal that you cooked or helped to cook. What was it, and who did you make it for?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I prefer cooking at home on most days. The main reason is money: as a student, I cannot afford to eat in restaurants very often, and a home-cooked meal costs less than half as much. Another reason is that I know exactly what is in my food, so I can use more vegetables and less oil. Cooking also helps me relax after a long day of classes. Of course, I still enjoy eating out with friends once or twice a month, especially when we want to try food from another country. But for everyday meals, my own kitchen is the better choice.

listening.script: Thanks. Now let's talk about your routine. Some people like to cook at home most days, while others prefer to eat out or order food. Which do you prefer, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: No, I don't agree. I think eating together is more important now exactly because everyone is so busy. During the day, the people in a family are in different places, and in the evening they often look at their own screens. A shared meal may be the only time when they really talk to each other. In my family, dinner was the moment when my parents found out what was happening at school, and when my sister and I heard their stories from work. It does not have to happen every day, and the food does not have to be special. Even two or three meals a week can keep a family close.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people think that eating meals together as a family is less important now than it was in the past, because everyone is so busy. Do you agree with this view? Why or why not?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I believe schools should teach every student to cook a few basic meals. Cooking is a life skill, just like managing money, and not all children can learn it at home, because many parents work long hours. Students who know how to prepare simple dishes will be able to eat well and save money when they live alone for the first time. Cooking classes are also a practical way to learn about other subjects, for example measuring in mathematics or how heat changes food in science. The lessons would not need much time. One hour a week for a single school year would probably be enough to give young people confidence in the kitchen.

listening.script: Here is my final question. Do you think schools should teach all students how to cook basic meals? Why or why not?
